ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This and the following studies were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Paris School of Economics (Approval number: 2023-052).
All participants provided their informed consent before participating in the study.

At T1, participants were randomly assigned to watch either a brief neuroplasticity video or a duration-matched control video on workplace safety (see section Videos below), read text summarizing the video, and answer some comprehension questions about the materials.
We recruited a total sample of 420 participants, allowing for 30 participants per condition (2) and disorder (7) combination.

Participants for this and the following studies were UK resident adults with English as their first language, recruited via Prolific Academic. 6 participants were excluded due to failing the attention check at the beginning of the study (reading a text and entering specific words into a text box) or failing to complete the study, resulting in a final sample of N = 414, primarily non-students (371 non-students, 43 students), with a mean age of 45.

We matched the sample size to Study 1 (N = 420). 9 participants were excluded due to failing the attention check at the beginning of the study (reading a text and entering specific words into a text box) or failing to complete the study, resulting in a final sample of N = 411 at T1, primarily non-students (381 non-students, 30 students), with a mean age of 44.

As a measure of behavioral intentions, we used the attitudinal social distance toward people with mental disorders scale (introduced by Link et al., 1999): Participants were asked how willing they would be to (1 = definitely not,4 = definitely): 1.

After completing the intervention part of the study, participants were informed that they would take part in the second study.
Participants were informed that they would participate in two separate studies.
In the first part of the study, participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: intervention or control.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We recruited a total sample of 420 participants, allowing for 30 participants per condition (2) and disorder (7) combination. This comfortably exceeded the sample size required for 80% power for a small effect size in the MANOVA (f²=0.06) and allowed us to capture possible interaction effects between condition and disorder category and to account for possible dropouts between T1 and T2.

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: alpha_level, software ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "apriori", statistical_test = "MANOVA", sample_size = 420, alpha_level = NA_real_, power = 0.8, effect_size = 0.06, effect_size_metric = "other", software = NA_character_), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "We recruited a total sample of 420 participants, allowing for 30 participants per condition (2) and disorder (7) combination. This comfortably exceeded the sample size required for 80% power for a small effect size in the MANOVA (f²=0.06) and allowed us to capture possible interaction effects between condition and disorder category and to account for possible dropouts between T1 and T2."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

stat_check.title: StatCheck
stat_check.summary_text: 1 possible error in t-tests or F-tests

table.text: Participants in the intervention condition reported significantly higher neuroplasticity knowledge scores (M = 78.14, SD = 8.96) than participants in the control condition (M = 72.53, SD = 12.2), t(87.86) = 2.61, p = .005, Cohen's d = 0.52.

However, there was a significant interaction with time: the effect of condition on recovery perceptions was present at T1 but not at T2 (binteraction = -0.386, SE = 0.109, t(401.08) = -3.54, p < .001; Table 4).

report: We detected possible errors in test statistics. Note that as the accuracy of statcheck has only been validated for *t*-tests and *F*-tests. report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p-values > 0.05", Text = "We also fitted five separate models, one for each item on the attitudinal social distance scale, but the effect of condition was not significant in any model (all p-values > 0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

table.text: p-values > 0.05

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p-values > 0.05", Sentence = "We also fitted five separate models, one for each item on the attitudinal social distance scale, but the effect of condition was not significant in any model (all p-values > 0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1345 columns across 33 data files.
#### Issues Identified

62 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

278 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **278 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: This and the following studies were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Paris School of Economics (Approval number: 2023-052).
live_data_statements: All participants provided their informed consent before participating in the study.

At T1, participants were randomly assigned to watch either a brief neuroplasticity video or a duration-matched control video on workplace safety (see section Videos below), read text summarizing the video, and answer some comprehension questions about the materials.
We recruited a total sample of 420 participants, allowing for 30 participants per condition (2) and disorder (7) combination.

Participants for this and the following studies were UK resident adults with English as their first language, recruited via Prolific Academic. 6 participants were excluded due to failing the attention check at the beginning of the study (reading a text and entering specific words into a text box) or failing to complete the study, resulting in a final sample of N = 414, primarily non-students (371 non-students, 43 students), with a mean age of 45.

We matched the sample size to Study 1 (N = 420). 9 participants were excluded due to failing the attention check at the beginning of the study (reading a text and entering specific words into a text box) or failing to complete the study, resulting in a final sample of N = 411 at T1, primarily non-students (381 non-students, 30 students), with a mean age of 44.

As a measure of behavioral intentions, we used the attitudinal social distance toward people with mental disorders scale (introduced by Link et al., 1999): Participants were asked how willing they would be to (1 = definitely not,4 = definitely): 1.

Two participants were excluded due to failing the attention check at the beginning of the study (reading a text and entering specific words into a text box) or failing to complete the study, resulting in a final sample of N = 418, primarily non-students (376 non-students, 42 students), with a mean age of 38.
After completing the intervention part of the study, participants were informed that they would take part in the second study.
Participants were informed that they would participate in two separate studies.
In the first part of the study, participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: intervention or control.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 14 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:14, File = c("S1_intervention_analysis copy.R", 
"S1_intervention_wrangling copy.R", "s2_t1_data_analysis.R", 
"s2_t2_intervention_data_wrangling.R", "s2_t3_wrangling.R", "s2_assignment_to_cond.R", 
"study 2 intervention data analysis.R", "s3_t1+t2+t3_wrangling.R", 
"s3_t1+t2_wrangling.R", "s3_t1_wrangling.R", "s3_t2_ids.R", "s3_data analysis.R", 
"interv_pooled_data_s2_s3.R", "s3_wrangling.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "—", "s2_t2_intervention_data_wrangling.R", "—", 
"S1_intervention_analysis copy.R", "—", "—", "—", "s3_t1+t2_wrangling.R, s3_t1_wrangling.R, s3_t1+t2+t3_wrangling.R", 
"s3_t1+t2+t3_wrangling.R, study 2 intervention data analysis.R", 
"s3_data analysis.R", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", 
"numeric", "numeric", "dependency", "numeric", "dependency", 
"numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "dependency", "dependency", 
"dependency", "numeric")), row.names = c(NA, -14L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Missing inputs
5 input files the code reads are in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("s1_intervention_data.rdata", "prolific_dems_study1.csv", 
"raw_intervention_study_1_labels.csv", "raw_intervention_study_1_numbers.csv", 
"s2_t1_clean_data.rdata"), Status = c("absent", "absent", "absent", 
"absent", "absent"), Reason = c("referenced file is not present in the repository, but a similarly-named file exists: s1_intervention_data copy.rdata", 
"referenced file is not present in the repository, but a similarly-named file exists: prolific_dems_study1 copy.csv", 
"referenced file is not present in the repository, but a similarly-named file exists: raw_intervention_study_2_t1_labels.csv", 
"referenced file is not present in the repository, but a similarly-named file exists: raw_intervention_study_2_t1_numbers.csv", 
"referenced file is not present in the repository, but a similarly-named file exists: s3_t1_clean_data.rdata"
)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 14 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `control_adhd_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `interv_adhd_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `control_asd_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `interv_asd_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `control_anorexia_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `interv_anorexia_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `control_bipolar_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `interv_bipolar_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `control_depression_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `interv_depression_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `control_schizophrenia_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `interv_s2_t2_schizophrenia_numbers.csv`, `control_ocd_s2_t2_numbers.csv`, `interv_ocd_s2_t2_numbers.csv`.
#### Files not run on their own
1 file is empty, so there is nothing to run, and it is not counted as a script: s3_wrangling.R.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 13 scripts: 5 ran without error, 8 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **2 scripts use an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `study 2 intervention data analysis.R` after `S1_intervention_analysis copy.R`; `s3_data analysis.R` after `study 2 intervention data analysis.R`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first; a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}
# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("S1_intervention_analysis copy.R", "S1_intervention_wrangling copy.R", 
"s2_t1_data_analysis.R", "s2_t2_intervention_data_wrangling.R", 
"s2_t3_wrangling.R", "s2_assignment_to_cond.R", "study 2 intervention data analysis.R", 
"s3_t1+t2+t3_wrangling.R", "s3_t1+t2_wrangling.R", "s3_t1_wrangling.R", 
"s3_t2_ids.R", "s3_data analysis.R", "interv_pooled_data_s2_s3.R", 
"s3_wrangling.R"), Outcome = c("errored", "errored", "errored", 
"errored", "ran_ok", "errored", "errored", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", 
"ran_ok", "errored", "errored", "ran_ok", "empty"), Detail = c("runtime", 
"runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "", "runtime", "runtime", "",

2.8, 4, 2.9, 2.6, 2, 5.3, 3.1, 2.9, 3.3, 5.4, 4.7, 6.6, 0)), row.names = c(NA, 
-14L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "s3_t2_ids.R", "Missing variable" = "s3_t1_t2_data_merged", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`library()` calls added**

**1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run it we added the `library()` calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after adding `library()` calls it should make itself**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "s3_t2_ids.R", "library() calls added" = "library(tidyverse), library(tidyr), library(car), library(effectsize), library(lme4), library(lmerTest), library(emmeans), library(flextable), library(patchwork), library(ggplot2), library(dplyr)"), row.names = "s3_t2_ids.R", class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

text.text: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery.
We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain's capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs.

Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control.
The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2.
The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall.
The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders.
In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance.

These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.
Over the past decades, mental disorders have increasingly been framed as rooted in the brain (Conrad & Slodden, 2013; Guley et al., 2026; Lebowitz & Appelbaum, 2019).
text.formatted: Over the past decades, mental disorders have increasingly been framed as rooted in the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Conrad & Slodden, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Guley et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Lebowitz & Appelbaum, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The logic behind this framing is simple: if a disorder can be shown to have a physical seat in the brain, it becomes harder to dismiss as a matter of willpower or moral flaw (Jefferson, 2022).
text.formatted: The logic behind this framing is simple: if a disorder can be shown to have a physical seat in the brain, it becomes harder to dismiss as a matter of willpower or moral flaw <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Jefferson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Using brain framing is sometimes motivated by the hope that portraying mental disorders as organic conditions would reduce blame and stigma toward the disorders and increase adherence to treatment (Lebowitz & Appelbaum, 2019).
text.formatted: Using brain framing is sometimes motivated by the hope that portraying mental disorders as organic conditions would reduce blame and stigma toward the disorders and increase adherence to treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lebowitz & Appelbaum, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The framing may have contributed to more people seeing mental disorders as "real" issues, which has decreased stigma and increased help-seeking in patients (Haslam & Tse, 2025).
text.formatted: The framing may have contributed to more people seeing mental disorders as "real" issues, which has decreased stigma and increased help-seeking in patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Haslam & Tse, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, neurobiological explanations of mental disorders have mixed consequences: while they may reduce blame toward affected people, they also promote beliefs that mental disorders are more immutable, less prone to recovery, and more effectively treated with drugs than psychotherapy (Guley et al., 2026; Haslam & Kvaale, 2015; Kvaale et al., 2013; Lebowitz & Appelbaum, 2019).
text.formatted: However, neurobiological explanations of mental disorders have mixed consequences: while they may reduce blame toward affected people, they also promote beliefs that mental disorders are more immutable, less prone to recovery, and more effectively treated with drugs than psychotherapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Guley et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Haslam & Kvaale, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Kvaale et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Lebowitz & Appelbaum, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, people appear to hold a specific essentialist bias toward mental disorders framed in neurobiological terms, treating "brain disorders" as innate in a similar way they reason about human biology in general (Berent & Platt, 2021).
text.formatted: Moreover, people appear to hold a specific essentialist bias toward mental disorders framed in neurobiological terms, treating "brain disorders" as innate in a similar way they reason about human biology in general <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Berent & Platt, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Most important for treatment-seeking, neurobiological attributions have been shown to reduce people's confidence in the effectiveness of psychotherapy, presumably because a "talk-based" intervention seems poorly matched to a disorder understood as a fixed biological defect (Perricone & Ahn, 2023).
text.formatted: Most important for treatment-seeking, neurobiological attributions have been shown to reduce people's confidence in the effectiveness of psychotherapy, presumably because a "talk-based" intervention seems poorly matched to a disorder understood as a fixed biological defect <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Perricone & Ahn, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, educational interventions teaching neuroplasticity -the brain's capacity to reorganize itself structurally and functionally throughout life in response to experience, learning, and intervention (Sarrasin et al., 2018) -have been widely used to challenge the views of human intelligence as fixed (Dweck, 2017).
text.formatted: On the other hand, educational interventions teaching neuroplasticity -the brain's capacity to reorganize itself structurally and functionally throughout life in response to experience, learning, and intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Sarrasin et al., 2018)</ref> -have been widely used to challenge the views of human intelligence as fixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Dweck, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These interventions are designed to cultivate a growth mindset, the belief that intelligence and abilities can be developed through effort and experience, by demonstrating that the brain itself remains capable of change (Dweck, 2017; Yeager & Dweck, 2020).
text.formatted: These interventions are designed to cultivate a growth mindset, the belief that intelligence and abilities can be developed through effort and experience, by demonstrating that the brain itself remains capable of change <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Dweck, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Yeager & Dweck, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analyses show that such interventions produce small but reliable improvements in motivation and learning outcomes (Burnette et al., 2023; Sarrasin et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Meta-analyses show that such interventions produce small but reliable improvements in motivation and learning outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Burnette et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Sarrasin et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: No study, to our knowledge, has connected these two literatures.

If the central harm of neurobiological framing of mental disorders is that it leads people to believe that the disorder is fixed, then neuroplasticity education, which teaches that the brain is not fixed, is a candidate intervention to reverse these negative effects.

Teaching people that the brain remains malleable even in adulthood should, in principle, counteract the prognostic pessimism documented by Haslam and Kvaale (2015) and Lebowitz and Appelbaum (2019), and could plausibly restore confidence in psychotherapy specifically, echoing findings that explanations of how psychotherapy changes the brain increase people's perceived confidence in its effectiveness (Perricone et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Teaching people that the brain remains malleable even in adulthood should, in principle, counteract the prognostic pessimism documented by <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Haslam and Kvaale (2015)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Lebowitz and Appelbaum (2019)</ref>, and could plausibly restore confidence in psychotherapy specifically, echoing findings that explanations of how psychotherapy changes the brain increase people's perceived confidence in its effectiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Perricone et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such shifts may not stop at belief: if perceived fixedness of the disorder drives desire for social distance (Haslam & Kvaale, 2015), then undermining that perception could plausibly extend to behavioral intentions -willingness to interact with, support, or avoid people with mental disorders.
text.formatted: Such shifts may not stop at belief: if perceived fixedness of the disorder drives desire for social distance <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Haslam & Kvaale, 2015)</ref>, then undermining that perception could plausibly extend to behavioral intentions -willingness to interact with, support, or avoid people with mental disorders.

text.text: The present paper brings together these bodies of literature to address two questions through three preregistered experiments.
First, does a short neuroplasticity educational intervention shift beliefs about whether brain-framed mental disorders are amenable to change and treatable through psychotherapy?
Second, does this shift extend beyond belief to behavioral intentions -willingness to engage in social contact and support -toward people with mental disorders?

The objective of this study was to determine whether a short educational intervention on neuroplasticity (watching a video, reading a short text summary of the video, and answering multiple-choice questions about the text and video) can influence the general public's beliefs regarding the efficacy of drug and psychotherapy treatments, and the potential for recovery, as compared to a control group, in the context of a mental disorder presented in brain terms.

In this and subsequent studies, we focused on seven prevalent mental disorder categories that differ in symptoms, duration, and the age of symptom onset: anorexia nervosa, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and schizophrenia (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).
Our research questions did not concern differences between disorders; rather the inclusion of multiple disorders was a methodological move to increase the generalizability of the conclusions.
We exposed one group of participants to a video intervention teaching them about neuroplasticity (intervention condition) and another group to an unrelated but matched video (control condition).
We measured beliefs about one of the disorders immediately after viewing the videos (T1) and beliefs about another disorder a week later (T2).
Our predictions were: P1.
Participants in the intervention condition will report higher perceived psychotherapy efficacy than those in the control condition.
Participants in the intervention condition will show a difference in perceived drug treatment efficacy compared with participants in the control condition. (open prediction about the direction) P3.
Participants in the intervention condition will report a higher perceived possibility of recovery than the participants in the control condition.
We tested each of these predictions at T1 and again at T2 to determine whether any intervention effects persisted.
Preregistration and data availability.
All hypotheses, the analysis plan, and materials were preregistered at: https://osf.io/ukcy5/overview.
text.formatted: All hypotheses, the analysis plan, and materials were preregistered at: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/ukcy5/overview">https://osf.io/ukcy5/overview</ref>.

text.text: Data and code are available via: https://osf.io/nb5sh/overview.
text.formatted: Data and code are available via: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/nb5sh/overview">https://osf.io/nb5sh/overview</ref>.

text.text: This and the following studies were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Paris School of Economics (Approval number: 2023-052).
All participants provided their informed consent before participating in the study.
The study used a between-subjects 2 (condition: intervention, control) × 7 (disorder) design.

At T1, participants were randomly assigned to watch either a brief neuroplasticity video or a duration-matched control video on workplace safety (see section Videos below), read text summarizing the video, and answer some comprehension questions about the materials.
They then read a vignette describing one of seven mental disorders as a brain disorder and rated familiarity, perceived drug treatment efficacy, psychotherapy efficacy, and possibility of recovery.
One week later, at T2, they completed the same measures for a different disorder.
Detailed procedure and vignette texts are available in Supplementary Materials.
To verify whether our intervention increased participants' knowledge of neuroplasticity, we conducted a pilot study (N = 100; 50 participants per condition).

Participants read eight statements from the neuroplasticity knowledge scale (adapted from Gholami et al., 2022, available in the Supplementary Materials) and indicated the extent to which they agreed with each one on a scale from 0 (completely disagree) to 100 (completely agree).
text.formatted: Participants read eight statements from the neuroplasticity knowledge scale (adapted from <ref type="bibr">Gholami et al., 2022, available</ref> in the Supplementary Materials) and indicated the extent to which they agreed with each one on a scale from 0 (completely disagree) to 100 (completely agree).

text.text: We compared total neuroplasticity knowledge scale scores between the intervention and control conditions using a one-tailed t-test.

Participants in the intervention condition reported significantly higher neuroplasticity knowledge scores (M = 78.14, SD = 8.96) than participants in the control condition (M = 72.53, SD = 12.2), t(87.86) = 2.61, p = .005, Cohen's d = 0.52.
When removing 3 participants who failed the attention questions after the video/text (had a score < 3 correct answers out of 5), Cohen's d = 0.55.
text.formatted: When removing 3 participants who failed the attention questions after the video/text (had a score < 3 correct answers out of 5), Cohen's d = 0.55.

text.text: We recruited a total sample of 420 participants, allowing for 30 participants per condition (2) and disorder (7) combination.

This comfortably exceeded the sample size required for 80% power for a small effect size in the MANOVA (f²=0.06) and allowed us to capture possible interaction effects between condition and disorder category and to account for possible dropouts between T1 and T2.
Participants.

Participants for this and the following studies were UK resident adults with English as their first language, recruited via Prolific Academic. 6 participants were excluded due to failing the attention check at the beginning of the study (reading a text and entering specific words into a text box) or failing to complete the study, resulting in a final sample of N = 414, primarily non-students (371 non-students, 43 students), with a mean age of 45.
The sample was balanced by sex (205 male and 204 female participants; 5 participants did not specify their sex).
Participants received £1.60 for taking part in T1 and £0.50 for T2.
Videos.
Videos for the intervention and control conditions, along with subtitles, were created and provided for use in this project by Sentis, a psychology-based safety culture consulting company.
Both videos used the same voiceover and graphics and were the same length.
The intervention video (available at: https://youtu.be/dOfuBNumrY0) describes the general principles of neuroplasticity without mentioning mental disorders.
text.formatted: The intervention video (available at: <ref type="url" target="https://youtu.be/dOfuBNumrY0">https://youtu.be/dOfuBNumrY0</ref>) describes the general principles of neuroplasticity without mentioning mental disorders.

text.text: The control video (available at: https://youtu.be/NXYCGgKlyPo) described an unrelated topic-workplace safety-without mentioning either neuroplasticity or mental disorders.
text.formatted: The control video (available at: <ref type="url" target="https://youtu.be/NXYCGgKlyPo">https://youtu.be/NXYCGgKlyPo</ref>) described an unrelated topic-workplace safety-without mentioning either neuroplasticity or mental disorders.

text.text: Data were analyzed in R. For each outcome variable, we fitted linear mixed models with condition, time, disorder, their interactions (condition × disorder and condition × time), and familiarity as fixed predictors, and a random effect of participant.
If the familiarity or interaction effects were not significant, we removed them from the final model.

Continuous outcome variables for this and the following studies were standardized before analysis, so regression coefficients for categorical predictors represent differences in standard deviation units of the outcome.
Descriptive statistics.
Table 1 presents descriptive statistics for the dependent variables by condition and time point.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> presents descriptive statistics for the dependent variables by condition and time point.

text.text: Prediction testing.
Table 2 summarises the ANOVA results.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> summarises the ANOVA results.

text.text: The main effect of condition on perceived psychotherapy treatment efficacy (P1) was not significant (b = -0.01, SE = 0.08; Figure 1A), but the effects of disorder and time were significant.
text.formatted: The main effect of condition on perceived psychotherapy treatment efficacy (P1) was not significant (b = -0.01, SE = 0.08; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>), but the effects of disorder and time were significant.

text.text: There was no significant main effect of the condition on perceived drug treatment efficacy (P2) (b = -0.14, SE = 0.09; Figure 1B).
text.formatted: There was no significant main effect of the condition on perceived drug treatment efficacy (P2) (b = -0.14, SE = 0.09; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>).

The results of Study 1 provided only limited support for our predictions.
Participants who received the neuroplasticity intervention perceived mental disorders as more amenable to recovery immediately after the intervention, but this difference disappeared one week later.
Contrary to our prediction, the intervention did not increase perceived efficacy of psychotherapy.

Although there was no overall effect on perceived drug treatment efficacy, participants in the intervention condition showed a greater increase in these ratings from T1 to T2 than participants in the control condition.
There was significant variation in outcomes across disorders, meaning that participants saw each disorder as differently amenable to treatment and recovery.
Greater familiarity with the disorder predicted greater perceptions of recovery.

Overall, these findings suggest that a brief one-shot neuroplasticity intervention can temporarily increase perceived recovery potential of mental disorders, but this disappears within one week, and there are no effects on beliefs about treatment efficacy.
We designed Study 2 as a follow-up to Study 1 to test whether reinforcing the neuroplasticity intervention would produce more durable and consequential changes in beliefs.
This approach was motivated by evidence that "two-shot" interventions generally produce more persistent effects than single-session ("one-shot") interventions (Maertens et al., 2025).

text.text: Study 2 replicated the positive immediate effect of the neuroplasticity intervention on perceived recovery.
Moreover, with the intervention booster, the effect persisted for at least seven days after the final exposure (14 days from first exposure).
Participants in the intervention condition of Study 2 consistently viewed mental disorders as more amenable to recovery than participants in the control condition across all three time points.
As in Study 1, the intervention did not influence beliefs about the effectiveness of psychotherapy or drug treatment.
Together, these findings suggest that neuroplasticity education changes expectations about recovery more readily than beliefs about how mental disorders should be treated.

Overall, these outcomes suggest that neuroplasticity education can increase expectations about recovery from mental disorders.

text.text: Across three preregistered studies, we tested whether a brief educational intervention on neuroplasticity could counter that pessimism in the general public.

Teaching people that the brain remains changeable throughout life increased positive expectations of recovery from mental disorders (Studies 1 and 2, and pooled analysis of Studies 2 and 3), but left confidence in psychotherapy and pharmaceutical treatment, and attitudes toward people with mental disorders, unmoved (Studies 1-3).

To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that neuroplasticity education, long used in classrooms to convince students that intelligence can grow (Burnette et al., 2023; Dweck, 2017), also shifts how the public reasons about recovery from mental disorders.

text.text: This finding has practical implications, as it suggests that one unintended consequence of neurobiological framing -reduced optimism about recovery -can be partially countered through a brief educational intervention (Haslam & Kvaale, 2015; Jefferson, 2022; Lebowitz & Appelbaum, 2019).

These findings align with previous research which shows that treatment preferences are driven more by causal beliefs about the disorder than by beliefs about prognosis (Lebowitz & Appelbaum, 2019; Perricone et al., 2024): learning that brains are malleable may widen what people think is possible without telling them which treatment gets them there.

text.text: Familiarity can be seen here as a stand-in for such contact, or for having had direct experience of the condition.

The fact that the intervention affected people's views regarding their recovery prospects but had no impact on their beliefs about treatment efficacy or their social distance attitudes can be explained by the literature on folk beliefs.

When confronted with new information, people do not do so as if they were starting from scratch: their existing lay theories concerning the causes of behavior influence the way in which they interpret new information (see Nettle et al., 2023), and new information generally coexists with rather than replaces these earlier intuitions (Shtulman & Valcarcel, 2012).

Modern workers seek environments where they not only remain physically safe but also feel included, supported, and engaged, prompting a broader understanding of what safety truly entails.

Safety is now seen as multidimensional, shaped by physical conditions, social interactions, and psychological well-being; the environment and tasks define physical safety, relationships influence social safety, and mental health and emotional security underpin psychological safety.

Negative experiences in any of these areas reduce focus, motivation, and the ability to work safely, while positive experiences foster calmness, collaboration, and engagement, allowing individuals and organizations to thrive.

Studies 2 and 3 intervention booster text Intervention group: "Until recently, people believed that the brain became largely fixed after childhood, with neural pathways that were stable and resistant to change.
More recent research has shown that this assumption was incorrect.
Neuroplasticity describes the brain's lifelong capacity to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections and adjusting existing ones in response to learning, experience, and injury.
Rather than being static, the brain functions as a highly interconnected network composed of billions of pathways that are activated with each thought, emotion, or action.
Pathways that are used frequently become stronger and more efficient, forming the neural basis of established habits and behaviors.
When a person begins to think or act in new ways, new neural connections start to develop.
With repeated activation, these new pathways are reinforced, whereas connections that are not used tend to weaken over time.
This strengthening and weakening of connections reflects neuroplasticity in action.
This capacity for change means that adults can learn new skills, modify habits, and adjust emotional responses.
People who have replaced an old habit or adopted a new way of thinking have experienced neuroplasticity directly.
Through sustained attention and repeated practice, individuals can intentionally promote the development of new neural patterns.

In sum, the adult brain remains adaptable throughout life; habits and patterns of thought correspond to neural pathways that can be reshaped; lasting change requires deliberate and repeated effort; and neuroplasticity supports learning, recovery after brain injury, and changes in behavior."
"Until recently, workplace safety was primarily defined as physical protection and the prevention of injury.
This perspective has been essential in ensuring that employees avoid accidents and return home unharmed.
However, expectations in today's workplaces have expanded beyond this narrow definition.
Employees look for work settings where they are not only physically protected but also feel valued, supported, and involved.
As a result, safety is increasingly understood as a multidimensional concept.

It encompasses physical safety, which is shaped by the work environment and job demands; social safety, which depends on the quality of interpersonal relationships; and psychological safety, which is grounded in emotional security and mental well-being.
When people experience problems in any of these areas, their concentration, motivation, and ability to perform tasks safely can decline.
In contrast, positive experiences promote a sense of stability, cooperation, and engagement, enabling both individuals and organizations to function more effectively.
Adopting this view of safety enhances resilience, improves performance, and encourages shared responsibility.
In this broader framework, safety is no longer seen merely as compliance with regulations but as a core element of organizational culture.

Fostering a positive safety climate becomes a strategic priority, contributing to employee well-being, supporting adaptability during change, and generating benefits that extend to clients and the wider community.
As work continues to change, safety must be understood as an evolving and inclusive construct that addresses fundamental human needs.
Integrating well-being into daily practices and regularly assessing and refining safety measures through feedback are essential.

When safety is treated as a holistic experience rather than a limited checklist of rules, it becomes a central driver of organizational quality and a foundation for workplaces in which people can truly flourish."

There are several limitations in our studies.
The intervention was intentionally brief and generic -a single (or boosted) lesson in neuroplasticity as a general brain property, not customized for any one disorder.
A longer, repeated, or disorder-specific program might produce larger and more durable effects.
Also, all outcomes relied on self-report from a UK online sample, limiting what we can say about actual behavior or about other populations.

Future research should test whether changes in recovery beliefs translate into real treatment decisions or attitudes, and whether disorder-specific interventions, for example, explaining the brain's role in ADHD or in schizophrenia specifically, strengthen the effect.
Neuroplasticity education is a promising, low-cost tool for raising public optimism about recovery, but hope is not the same as reduced social distance.
A single lesson about the brain moved one belief and left the other beliefs and attitudes -confidence in treatment efficacy, willingness to maintain social distance -standing.

Future interventions may therefore be most effective if they combine neuroplasticity education with disorder-specific childhood, with fixed neural pathways resistant to change, but recent research shows the opposite.
Neuroplasticity is the brain's lifelong ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections and modifying existing ones in response to learning, experience, and injury.
The brain functions like a dynamic power grid with billions of interconnected pathways that activate with every thought, feeling, or action.
Frequently used pathways become strong and efficient, representing established habits and behaviors, while new ways of thinking or acting begin to carve out new pathways.
Repeated use strengthens these new routes, while old, unused ones weaken, illustrating neuroplasticity in action.
This adaptability means adults can learn new skills, change habits, and alter emotional responses; anyone who has ever overcome a bad habit or shifted their mindset has experienced it firsthand.
With sustained attention and repetition, individuals can intentionally rewire their brains to adopt new patterns.
